questions.q: What are the five standard stages of narrative structure in a short story, and which event in "The Rocking-horse Winner" marks the transition from exposition to rising action?
questions.a: The five stages are exposition, rising action, climax, falling action, and resolution. The transition from exposition to rising action occurs when Paul, after learning his father has "no luck," begins his secret rocking-horse rides to find luck himself (Paragraph: "He went off by himself... seeking for the clue to 'luck'"). A wrong answer that identifies the birthday gift or the first bet as the transition reveals the student cannot distinguish the protagonist's internal commitment (the true structural turning point) from external plot events.

questions.q: Explain in your own words how the recurring whisper "There must be more money" functions as a structural device rather than merely a thematic motif.
questions.a: The whisper acts as a structural metronome: it appears at the end of exposition to establish the central conflict, resurges after the birthday gift to show the failure of the first solution (rising action complication), and intensifies to a "chorus of frogs" before the Derby to signal the final crisis. A student who describes it only as a symbol of greed misses its rhythmic role in pacing the narrative and marking each structural phase.

questions.q: Apply the concept of "in media res" to the opening of the story. Does "The Rocking-horse Winner" begin in media res? Justify with textual evidence.
questions.a: No, it does not begin in media res. The opening provides full exposition: the mother's background, the family's financial anxiety, the house's atmosphere, and the children's perception — all before Paul's first action. A story beginning in media res would open with Paul already riding the horse or placing a bet. A wrong answer claiming it starts in media res because "the whisper is already happening" confuses atmospheric tension with narrative chronology.

questions.q: Analyze how Lawrence uses parallelism between Paul's three major wins (Daffodil, Lively Spark, Malabar) to structure the rising action. What changes in each iteration?
questions.a: Each win escalates in stakes, secrecy, and physical toll: Daffodil (Lincoln) is a tentative test with Uncle Oscar as sole confidant; Lively Spark (Leger) expands the partnership to three and yields ten thousand pounds; Malabar (Derby) is a solitary, frenzied ride that kills him. The parallelism creates a tightening spiral — the intervals shorten, the amounts grow, and Paul's control diminishes. A student who only lists the horses misses the structural pattern of accelerating consequences.

questions.q: Evaluate the narrative decision to have Paul die immediately after the Derby win. Does this ending strengthen or weaken the story's critique of materialism? Defend your judgment.
questions.a: It strengthens the critique by making the acquisition of money literally fatal, turning the whisper's promise ("if you're lucky you will always get more money") into a deadly irony. The structure denies the reader a conventional resolution (family happiness with wealth) and forces confrontation with the cost. A wrong answer calling it "melodramatic" or "unnecessary" fails to see that the tragedy is the structural inevitable outcome of a plot built on the equation luck = money = life.

questions.q: Create a one-paragraph alternative ending where Paul survives the Derby. Ensure your version retains the story's narrative structure (i.e., still has a climax, falling action, resolution) but changes the thematic outcome.
questions.a: A strong response will keep the climax (the ride), falling action (mother's discovery), and resolution (uncle's comment) but alter the final irony — e.g., Paul lives but the whisper persists, or the money is lost, or the mother's heart remains hard. A weak answer that simply writes "Paul recovers and they live happily" discards the structural logic that the whisper is self-sustaining and cannot be silenced by money.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Plot is the sequence of events arranged in a cause-and-effect chain that constitutes the narrative, while narrative structure refers to the ______ framework (exposition, rising action, climax, falling action, resolution) and the techniques (foreshadowing, flashback, point of view) used to present that plot.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you are asked to explain why Paul dies right after winning eighty thousand pounds — a summary of events won't answer *why* the story is ______ that way.
What is Plot? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Plot is the sequence of events arranged in a cause-and-effect chain that constitutes the narrative, while narrative structure refers to the organizational framework (exposition, rising action, climax, falling action, resolution) and the techniques (foreshadowing, flashback, point of view) used to present that plot.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Plot?
questions.a: Students often identify the climax as the moment Paul wins the Derby (Malabar comes in first) because it is the peak of external action.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can identify and label the five structural stages in the story, explain how Lawrence uses the whispering house as a structural device to drive rising action, and articulate why the climax occurs at Paul's final ride rather than at the moment of winning the Derby.
